opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest risk is that you end up optimizing for the measurement rather than the capability. Reinforcement learning is extremely good at finding whatever signal you give it and pushing hard on it. If the reward comes from a benchmark, the model will learn to be very good at that benchmark, including all its quirks, its formats, and sometimes its loopholes. The number goes up, but that doesn't necessarily mean the model has become more useful or more intelligent in a general sense.

Current benchmarks are mostly static, well-defined, and verifiable: math problems with a single answer, coding tasks with unit tests, multiple-choice questions. That's convenient for RL, because you get a clean reward. But the real world isn't like that. Real tasks are long-horizon, ambiguous, and often have no single correct answer. They require the model to ask clarifying questions, plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, and judge when it's done. If you only train on what's easy to verify, you may produce a model that looks brilliant on a leaderboard but is brittle once you put it in a messy environment.

There's also a subtler issue. Once the whole field optimizes around the same handful of benchmarks, everyone's models start to look alike. You converge on the same behaviors and blind spots, and you lose the diversity of approaches that drives real progress. Benchmarks saturate quickly now, sometimes within months, so if your research agenda is defined by them, you're always chasing a target that's about to become irrelevant.

So what I care about more is building environments and reward signals that reflect what we actually want the model to do, things closer to real work, where the model has to act as an agent over many steps. That's much harder, because the reward is noisier and the environments are expensive to build. But I think that's where the real gains are. Benchmarks should be a sanity check, not the objective. If you treat them as the objective, you'll get very good at the test and not much else.

r001.rationale: It warns that optimizing for benchmarks means learning their quirks and loopholes, and says models converge around the same handful of benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It describes brittleness in messy real-world environments and weaker general usefulness, but does not clearly state a sharp performance drop on unseen tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest risk is that benchmarks become the objective rather than a measurement. Once you start doing RL directly against a fixed set of tasks, the model gets very good at exactly what's being measured, and you lose information about whether the underlying capability actually generalizes. The score goes up, but it stops telling you anything.

There's a more subtle version too. The benchmarks we have today reflect what we can easily verify right now: math problems with a single answer, coding tasks with unit tests. Those are great for RL because the reward is clean. But if the whole field optimizes toward them, we end up shaping intelligence around what happens to be checkable, not around what's actually useful. A lot of real work is long-horizon, open-ended, and doesn't have a ground truth you can grade in a few seconds. If we don't invest in those harder reward signals, we'll get models that are superhuman at contests and still awkward at the things people need.

So the way I think about it internally is that benchmarks are a sanity check, not a target. What we care about is whether the model learns something general through the RL process, something that transfers to tasks we never trained on. If a gain only shows up on the benchmark and nowhere else, that's a signal we've overfit the process, even if the number looks good. Ultimately the better test is whether users feel the difference in things they actually do.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether benchmark gains generalize and mentions transfer to unseen tasks, but it does not state that performance drops sharply on those tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the main risk is that we confuse improving a score with improving the underlying capability. A benchmark is only a proxy for what we actually want. If we optimize very aggressively against it, the model may learn strategies that work well for that particular distribution without becoming better at solving unfamiliar problems.

With reinforcement learning, this becomes especially important because the reward determines what behavior gets reinforced. If something valuable is missing from the reward—like recognizing that a question is ambiguous or knowing when to ask for more information—then a higher score doesn’t necessarily mean a more useful model.

So I think we need to keep asking: does the improvement transfer? Does it hold up on new tasks, with different formulations, and in longer interactions? Benchmarks are useful signals, but they shouldn’t become the definition of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response warns that a model may learn strategies for a benchmark’s particular distribution, but does not say training concentrates on a few isolated tasks.

r002.rationale: It says benchmark gains may not transfer to unfamiliar problems, but does not state that performance on unseen tasks drops sharply.

sol-6.1.text:
The risk is that we get very good at the benchmark without getting much better at the underlying capability we care about. In reinforcement learning, you need a reward signal, and benchmarks provide something convenient and measurable. But that signal is only a proxy. If you optimize it aggressively, the model may learn shortcuts that improve the score but don’t generalize.

So I think the important question is whether the improvement transfers. Can the model solve unfamiliar problems, operate in a different environment, or handle a task where the reward is harder to specify? Benchmark progress is useful evidence, but if we make it the objective, we can end up narrowing our research around what is easy to measure.
